lesson.text: Quick memory: what are the five steps of the design cycle? (Idea, plan, make, test, improve.) Today we plan, make and test structures.
A structure holds something up or keeps its shape: a bridge, a tower, a chair, a shelf. Whatever it must hold is called its load.
A frame structure is a skeleton of bars, like an electricity pylon, a climbing frame or a bicycle. A shell structure is a hollow outer skin, like an egg, a box or a helmet.
Triangles make the strongest frames. Push a square frame and it squashes into a diamond; add a diagonal bar to make two triangles, and it stays firm.
Paper and card get much stiffer when you fold, roll or layer them. A flat sheet flops, but a tube or a zigzag fold can hold up a book.
A wide base makes a tower steadier, and putting the heavy parts at the bottom helps it not topple over.
Stiff means it does not bend; strong means it does not break. Test by adding loads one at a time, like coins, and count how many it holds.
Try it in the world: build a bridge with a frame of triangles, like a real steel bridge, and a tall tower with a wide base. Look for triangles in the buildings around you!

exercises.prompt: Which shape makes a frame the strongest?
exercises.hint: Which frame did not squash when it was pushed?
exercises.explain: A triangle keeps its shape when pushed, so it is the strongest.

exercises.prompt: Is it a frame structure or a shell structure?
exercises.hint: A frame is bars; a shell is a hollow skin.
exercises.explain: Frames: a climbing frame, a bicycle, a pylon. Shells: an egg, a box, a helmet.

exercises.prompt: A square frame can be pushed out of shape easily.
exercises.hint: Look at the pushed square in the lesson.
exercises.explain: True: a square frame squashes into a diamond unless it is braced.

exercises.prompt: Which base makes a tower steadier?
exercises.hint: Would a wide or a narrow tower tip over more easily?
exercises.explain: A wide base is steadier, so the tower is harder to tip over.

exercises.prompt: How can you make a square frame stiff?
exercises.hint: Which shape does a diagonal make?
exercises.explain: A diagonal bar splits the square into two triangles, so it stays firm.

exercises.hint: Which one could stand up on its own?
choices: a sheet of paper rolled into a tube
exercises.explain: A rolled tube is much stiffer than a flat sheet of the same paper.

exercises.prompt: Folding card into a zigzag makes it stiffer.
exercises.hint: Think of the card inside a cardboard box.
exercises.explain: True: zigzag folds, like those inside cardboard, make card much stiffer.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.explain: Load: what it holds. Frame: a skeleton of bars. Shell: a hollow outer skin. Stiff: does not bend easily.

exercises.prompt: Why do bridges and cranes have so many triangles?
exercises.hint: What happened when the square was pushed?
choices: triangles keep their shape under a load
exercises.explain: A triangle cannot change shape unless a bar breaks, so triangles keep bridges and cranes firm.

exercises.prompt: Zara's tall tower keeps toppling over. What could help?
exercises.hint: Should the heavy parts and the width be at the top or the bottom?
exercises.explain: A wider base (and heavy parts at the bottom) makes the tower steadier.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between stiff and strong?
exercises.hint: Think of a ruler bending and snapping.
choices: stiff does not bend; strong does not break
exercises.explain: Something stiff does not bend much; something strong does not break.

exercises.prompt: Put a fair test of paper bridges in order.
exercises.hint: A fair test keeps everything the same but the thing you test.
items: record how many each one holds
add coins one at a time
put each one across the same gap
make bridges of the same paper and length
exercises.explain: Same paper and length, same gap, coins one at a time, then record how many each holds.

exercises.prompt: A shell structure has lots of bars inside, like a skeleton.
exercises.explain: False: that is a frame. A shell is a hollow outer skin, like an egg or a box.

exercises.prompt: Which of these frames will stay firm when pushed?
exercises.hint: Look for the frame made of triangles.
exercises.explain: B is braced with a diagonal into two triangles, so it stays firm.

exercises.prompt: Sort them: does it make a structure stronger and steadier, or weaker?
exercises.hint: Triangles, tubes, folds and wide bases help. What makes things bend or topple?
exercises.explain: Stronger or steadier: a diagonal bar (two triangles), a wider base, paper rolled into a tube. Weaker: a thin, pointy base and heavy parts at the top, which make it topple.

exercises.prompt: Order the paper supports from the weakest to the strongest.
exercises.hint: Folding and rolling make paper stiffer. Which shape is stiffest?
exercises.explain: A flat sheet flops, a sheet folded once is stiffer, and a rolled tube is stiffest of all: it can hold up a book.

exercises.prompt: Match each problem to the fix that helps most.
exercises.hint: Think of wide bases, triangles, folding and stiffness.
exercises.explain: A wider base stops a tower toppling. A diagonal bar turns a wobbly square into two firm triangles. Folding or rolling paper makes it stiff, so the bridge sags less. A thicker or stiffer shelf bends less.
